topicTitle: Critical Reasoning — Strengthen and Weaken Arguments

questions.question:
Argument: A company argues that its new training programme improves employee productivity, because output per employee in the department that took it rose by 15% in the following quarter.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: The company spent a large sum on the programme.
Output in a similar department that did not take the programme stayed unchanged in the same quarter.
Employees found the programme interesting.
Some employees left the company after the programme.
questions.explanation: A similar department without the programme showed no rise, which rules out a general cause and supports the programme.

questions.question:
Argument: A shop owner claims that the shop's loyalty card scheme increased sales, because sales rose after the scheme was introduced.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: A major festival season began the same week and sales rose at all shops in the area.
The scheme was advertised widely.
Customers often hold several loyalty cards.
The shop is located in a busy market.
questions.explanation: The festival season gives another explanation for the rise in sales, so it weakens the claim about the scheme.

questions.question:
Argument: A city should build more cycling tracks, since they will cut air pollution by encouraging people to cycle instead of driving.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Cycling is a popular sport in many countries.
Cycling tracks cost less than roads.
Some cities have no cycling tracks.
In cities that built cycling tracks, the share of people commuting by cycle rose and the number of car trips fell.
questions.explanation: It shows that tracks lead to more cycling and fewer car trips, which is the mechanism the argument relies on.

questions.question:
Argument: A city should build more cycling tracks, since they will cut air pollution by encouraging people to cycle instead of driving.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Cycling tracks need regular maintenance.
Many cyclists wear helmets.
Surveys show that most people who use the new tracks used to walk or take the bus, not drive.
Cycling tracks are popular on weekends.
questions.explanation: If the track users were not drivers, car use and pollution will not fall, which undermines the argument.

questions.question:
Argument: Students who eat breakfast score higher on tests, so schools should provide free breakfast to raise test scores.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Many students enjoy breakfast.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
In schools that began free breakfast, average test scores rose, while scores stayed flat in comparable schools that did not.
Some schools already provide lunch.
questions.explanation: A comparison between schools with and without free breakfast directly supports the claim that breakfast raises scores.

questions.question:
Argument: Students who eat breakfast score higher on tests, so schools should provide free breakfast to raise test scores.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Free breakfast is expensive for schools to run.
Students who eat breakfast also sleep longer and study more, and these habits account for their higher scores.
Some students dislike school meals.
Breakfast is eaten at home in most cases.
questions.explanation: If sleep and study explain the higher scores, providing breakfast alone may not raise scores, so the argument is weakened.

questions.question:
Argument: To reduce road accidents, the government plans to raise the fine for speeding.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: Drivers will slow down to avoid the higher fine.
All road accidents are caused by speeding.
Fines are the government's main source of income.
Speeding fines have never been raised before.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if drivers respond to the fine by slowing down. The other options are too strong or irrelevant.

questions.question:
Argument: The new highway will boost the economy of the towns along it, because more vehicles will pass through them.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: The highway has four lanes.
Highway construction created some jobs.
Several towns along the highway are small.
The highway bypasses the towns, so vehicles can reach their destinations without entering any town.
questions.explanation: If vehicles bypass the towns, the extra traffic will not pass through them, which breaks the link in the argument.

questions.question:
Argument: A drug is effective, because 80% of the patients who took it recovered within a week.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: The drug is expensive.
Most patients took the drug with water.
The drug was tested in many hospitals.
About 85% of patients with this illness recover within a week without any medicine.
questions.explanation: If more patients recover without the drug, the 80% figure does not show the drug works, so it weakens the argument.

questions.question:
Argument: A school will start classes at 9 a.m. instead of 8 a.m., since better-rested students learn more and students will be better rested.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: All students walk to school.
Teachers prefer a later start.
Students will actually sleep longer if classes begin later.
The school day will become shorter.
questions.explanation: The conclusion that students will be better rested depends on their actually sleeping more. Negate it and the plan loses its point.

questions.question:
Argument: Hotels in a hill town raised their room rates in summer, so the demand for rooms must be high in summer.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Hotels in the town are old.
Hotels in the town report that most rooms are fully booked weeks in advance in summer.
Room rates are lower in winter.
Many tourists carry their own food.
questions.explanation: Full advance bookings are direct evidence of high demand, which supports the conclusion.

questions.question:
Argument: The crime rate in a locality fell after extra police patrols began, so the patrols reduce crime.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: The crime rate fell by the same amount in neighbouring localities where no extra patrols began.
The patrols began in January.
The police increased patrols in the evening.
Residents welcomed the patrols.
questions.explanation: A similar fall elsewhere without patrols suggests another cause for the fall, which weakens the claim.

questions.question:
Argument: A company should switch to solar power because it will lower its electricity bills.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: The company's electricity bills are high, and the cost of installing solar panels would be recovered within three years from the savings.
Solar panels are made of silicon.
Some companies already use solar power.
The company's offices are on the third floor.
questions.explanation: It shows that bills are high and that savings repay the cost quickly, which supports the claim of lower bills.

questions.question:
Argument: A survey found that people who own pets report being happier than those who do not. A columnist concludes that owning a pet makes people happier.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Many pet owners spend time outdoors.
Pet food can be costly.
The survey included thousands of people.
People who are already happy are more likely to adopt and keep pets.
questions.explanation: This reverses the direction of cause: happiness may lead to pet ownership, so the survey does not show that pets cause happiness.

questions.question:
Argument: The city council argues that the new parking charges will reduce traffic in the city centre, because people will choose public transport instead of paying to park.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: The parking charges will raise a large amount of money.
Public transport is cheaper than driving for all trips.
Public transport is a practical alternative for those who now drive to the centre.
Everyone who drives to the centre parks on the street.
questions.explanation: The argument requires that people have a workable alternative; otherwise they would keep driving and paying.

questions.question:
Argument: Studies show that students who learn a musical instrument do better in mathematics. A teacher argues that music lessons improve mathematical ability.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Many students enjoy music lessons.
In an experiment, students randomly assigned to music lessons improved in mathematics more than students randomly assigned to art lessons.
Mathematics teachers often play instruments.
Music lessons cost more than art lessons.
questions.explanation: Random assignment removes the possibility that better students simply choose music, so it directly supports the causal claim.

questions.question:
Argument: The mayor claims the new flyover has cut travel time in the city, because the average time taken by buses on the route fell from 40 to 30 minutes.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: The flyover was built in two years.
At the same time, the bus route was shortened by about 25% when two stops were dropped.
The flyover has a speed limit of 60 km/h.
Bus fares on the route are unchanged.
questions.explanation: A route shortened by 25% would take about 30 minutes without any help from the flyover, so the fall in time may not be due to it.

questions.question:
Argument: The editor argues that the newspaper should stop its print edition, because most readers now read it online.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: The newspaper will not lose a significant share of its readers or revenue by ending the print edition.
Online readers are younger than print readers.
The print edition was started 50 years ago.
All print readers will switch to the online edition.
questions.explanation: The case for stopping print depends on not losing important readers or revenue. The last option is too strong; the argument needs only that losses are not significant.

questions.question:
Argument: A shop owner argues that offering discounts attracts customers who then buy full-priced items too, so discounts raise total profit.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Discounts are advertised in newspapers.
The shop offers discounts every festival.
Some customers prefer shopping online.
Customers who come for discounted items buy almost nothing else.
questions.explanation: If discount shoppers buy only discounted items, there are no extra full-price sales, which weakens the claim.

questions.question:
Argument: A bakery says its new no-added-sugar biscuit is healthier, because it contains 30 per cent fewer calories than the original biscuit.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: The new biscuit is available in three flavours.
The bakery has been open since 1990.
Customers eat twice as many of the new biscuits at a time because they believe the biscuits are healthier.
The packet of the new biscuit is green.
questions.explanation: If people eat twice as many, they may take in more calories overall, which undermines the claim that the new biscuit is healthier.
